transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been going on that brought you in today?

Well, hi. Yeah, thanks. I, uh, I guess I’m here because things have just been... really off lately, and it's starting to bleed into every part of my day. 

You see, I work down at the distribution center—I’ve been an inventory clerk there for years. I did some college back in the day, but ended up in logistics and I usually really like it. But a little while ago, they had this whole management reshuffle and they made me the acting workflow lead. Which, you know, sounds great on paper, right? It's supposed to be a good opportunity. But honestly, ever since they gave me that title, it’s just been a total nightmare for me. 

I wake up and I’m already dreading the shift. I literally walk into the warehouse and my shoulders are practically up to my ears, I’m just so incredibly tense before I even clock in. And I’m usually a pretty easygoing guy, but lately? Man, if one of the guys makes even a tiny mistake in the SAP system—like, just a minor data entry error, which happens all the time because SAP is super finicky and the scanners lag—I just snap at them. I completely lose my cool over these little SAP errors that I normally wouldn't think twice about. 

And the worst part is it’s affecting my actual performance. I'm responsible for the cycle-count deadlines, and I have *never* missed one. I pride myself on keeping the inventory straight, but now I’m missing those deadlines. I'm just dropping the ball left and right. 

Then, by the time my shift is finally over, I’m just... I have absolutely nothing left in the tank. I used to hit the courts and play pickup basketball with some buddies a couple of times a week to blow off steam, but I’m just way too drained for that now. I go home and I just sit there. I don’t even have the energy to work on my sketches anymore, and I love drawing, it’s always been my main way to unwind and clear my head. But now, nothing. I'm just completely wiped out all the time, and I don't really know how to get back to normal.
When did these feelings start in relation to the management reshuffle and your new role as acting workflow lead?

Well, so, the whole reshuffle thing actually kicked off right after we had this big team merger. Corporate decided they needed to combine the inbound receiving guys with the outbound logistics team to cut down on overhead or whatever, which, honestly, anyone who actually works on the floor could have told them was going to be a massive headache. So suddenly we have twice the people in the same space, half of them don't know the specific SAP modules we use for outbound, and management is just scrambling to put people in charge of the chaos. That's exactly when they pulled me into the office and gave me the acting workflow lead title. 

At first, for like the first couple of weeks, I thought the stress was just the normal growing pains of a merger, you know? You expect a little friction when you're combining two completely different warehouse cultures. But... I'd say within the first month or two, tops, I could really tell I just wasn't handling the work the way I normally do. 

I mean, normally I can just roll with the punches. If a truck is late or a pallet gets misplaced, I just track it down and fix it, no big deal. But right around that one or two-month mark, I started noticing that instead of just fixing the problem and moving on, I was carrying it with me. I remember it was right around the time they finalized the new combined shift schedules, maybe six or seven weeks in, and I was just sitting at my desk staring at the cycle-count sheets realizing that I wasn't just tired from the extra hours, I was completely overwhelmed by everything. It wasn't just a bad day or a bad week, it was becoming my new normal. And it just sort of crept up on me, because you always want to think you can handle it, right? You want to step up. But then a month or two goes by and you realize you're snapping at guys you've worked with for five years over absolute nonsense. So yeah, definitely within those first two months after the merger happened and I got the title, that's when it really became obvious to me that the wheels were coming off.
Have you noticed that you’re not getting the same enjoyment out of things you usually like, like basketball or drawing?

Yeah, exactly. It's not even just that I'm not getting the same enjoyment out of them, it's that I've completely stopped showing up for them altogether. I mean, I haven't been down to the courts in... man, it has to be weeks now. The guys have texted me a few times asking where I was, if I was sick or something, and I just sort of blew them off, which I feel terrible about. And my sketchbooks are just gathering dust on my nightstand. I used to pick one up every single night, just to doodle, you know? Just to get the warehouse out of my head and reset my brain. But now, I just stare at the wall. 

It really feels like work is just completely taking over my life. It's bleeding into everything. And the crazy thing is, even though it's taking up all my mental energy and ruining my free time, I'm not even doing a good job at the actual work! I know I mentioned dropping the ball on those cycle-count deadlines earlier, but it actually got bad enough that my supervisor had to pull me into the office for a formal performance check-in about it. Which, let me tell you, was incredibly humiliating. 

I've been at that center for years, I know our inventory flow inside and out, and suddenly I'm sitting in this little glass office having my supervisor bring up these missed deadlines like I'm some new hire who doesn't know what he's doing. It was awful. So yeah, the stress from the floor comes home with me, it drains absolutely all my energy for hoops or my usual sketching time, and then I go back to work the next day already exhausted, and then I drop the ball again, and end up in a performance check-in. It's just this massive, exhausting loop that's swallowed up everything I actually used to like doing.
When you say you’re not getting the same enjoyment out of things like basketball or drawing, does it feel like you’re not enjoying anything at all anymore, even things you used to really like?

I mean, no, it's not... it's not like the whole world has gone completely gray or anything dramatic like that. I wouldn't say it's *everything*. Like, if I'm just sitting on the couch and, I don't know, a really good game is on TV, or if I order a pizza from my favorite spot down the street—the one that does the really good deep dish with the caramelized crust—I definitely still enjoy that. I can still eat it and think, man, this is great. So the capacity to enjoy things is definitely still in my brain somewhere. 

It's really more of an energy thing, I think? Because with basketball, you know, you have to actually get your gear together, drive down to the park, deal with the guys arguing over foul calls, and physically run up and down the asphalt for an hour. It's a whole production. And even with my sketches, which sounds like it should be relaxing, it actually takes a lot of mental focus. Especially because I usually work in charcoal, which I love because you can get these really deep, rich shadows and contrasts, but it's super messy and you have to really pay attention to the lighting and the proportions on the page. If you mess up charcoal, it's a total nightmare to erase without smudging the whole sketchbook. 

So... yeah, I guess what I'm saying is, it's not that I wouldn't enjoy drawing or playing hoops if I magically had the energy for them. I'm pretty sure I still would. It's just that the warehouse, and dealing with all those SAP errors and trying to babysit the new outbound guys, it just drains my battery down to absolute zero by the time I clock out. So I only have the bandwidth for the easy stuff, you know? Just sitting there, maybe watching a movie. But I still enjoy the easy stuff, yeah. It's just the big things, my actual hobbies, that I'm too wiped out to even attempt right now.
Have you noticed that your mood has been down or low most of the day, nearly every day, not just during work or when something stressful happens?

No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's not... it's not like this constant dark cloud that just follows me around from the minute I wake up to the minute I go to sleep, regardless of what's happening. It's really, very specifically tied to the job and the stress of this whole reshuffle thing. 

Like, if you take the warehouse out of the equation, I'm actually okay. Take this past Saturday, for instance. I actually had a pretty good morning. I woke up, didn't have to set an alarm, which was great, and I just made myself some breakfast—just some eggs and toast, nothing crazy, but I took my time with it. I was sitting on the couch, drinking my coffee, and I felt completely normal. I wasn't down, I wasn't sad. I was just, you know, existing and feeling fine. 

But then... I don't know, maybe around two or three in the afternoon, I made the mistake of checking my phone, and I saw a text from one of the floor supervisors about a pallet of electronics that got routed to the wrong staging area on Friday night. And man, the second I read that text, it was just like... boom. My stomach dropped, my mood completely tanked, and I spent the rest of the day just dreading Monday morning and trying to figure out how I was going to untangle that mess in the SAP system. 

So it’s not that I’m just down for no reason all day, every day. If I can actually disconnect and not think about the inbound and outbound schedules, I feel like my old self. It’s just that the job is so chaotic right now that it feels like I’m always on call, or at least my brain thinks I am, so it's hard to get that distance. But yeah, the low mood is definitely there because of the work situation, not just some random sadness that happens all the time for no reason. If work was fixed, I'm pretty sure my mood would be totally fine.
Do you find yourself feeling anxious or overly worried about things, even when there’s no immediate problem at work or something specific to stress about?

No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, if there's no problem, I'm not just sitting around making problems up in my head, you know? I'm actually a pretty laid-back guy by nature. Like, outside of this whole warehouse nightmare, I don't really stress about much at all. 

Take my apartment, for example. My lease is up for renewal next month, right? And the property management company—they're this big corporate outfit that bought the building a couple of years ago, and they always jack up the rent. Usually by like fifty or seventy-five bucks, which is obviously annoying. I know a lot of people who would be pacing the floors worrying about that, trying to figure out if they need to pack up all their stuff, rent a truck, and move across town. But for me? I just looked at the renewal letter they taped to my door, did a quick budget in my head, and thought, alright, I'll just cut back on ordering out so much, maybe skip the deep dish pizza for a bit, and I'll make it work. I didn't lose a single wink of sleep over it. I just don't have that kind of brain that spirals about every little thing in life, or the news, or my health, or whatever else people get anxious about. 

But work... that's the only thing. If I'm feeling that knot in my chest or I'm keyed up, it is one hundred percent because I'm thinking about those cycle-counts, or the SAP system errors, or wondering if the new guys are completely botching the inbound freight while I'm not there to watch them. If you take the warehouse out of my brain, I'm totally fine. So, no, if there's no specific work problem hanging over my head, I'm not anxious at all. It really all just comes back to the floor.
